title: Short Stuff: Bed Sheet Ghosts
summary: Short Stuff episode on the origins of the bedsheet ghost costume. Chuck and Josh trace the image to burial shrouds and sheet-wrapped bodies in 17th–19th century Britain, describe the 1805 Hammersmith case in which bricklayer Thomas Millwood was killed by ghost hunter Francis Smith, who was pardoned by King George III, and cover how sheet ghosts moved into spiritualist double-exposure photos, stage performance, and cartoons like Casper and Mickey Mouse's "Lonesome Ghosts." They close with Halloween costume tips.

segments.title: Opening banter and 'spoopy'
segments.summary: Josh welcomes listeners ahead of Halloween and the hosts check whether 'spoopy' is a real word.

segments.title: Bedsheet ghost introduction and burial shrouds
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the bedsheet ghost as a nostalgic costume and pop culture staple. The hosts mention the film A Ghost Story and explain the link to 17th-century British burial shrouds and linen wrapping of the dead.

segments.title: Green burials and sheet-wearing thieves
segments.summary: Josh notes burial shrouds are back in green burials. The hosts say London thieves sometimes wore sheets to scare and rob people.

segments.title: Ghost panic and vigilante ghost hunters
segments.summary: The hosts discuss ghost panic in early 1800s London, with citizens hunting ghosts and criminals in sheets.

segments.title: Thomas Millwood and Francis Smith case
segments.summary: Josh describes the Hammersmith case: Francis Smith, hunting ghosts, encountered bricklayer Thomas Millwood, who always wore white and refused to change despite his wife's warnings. Millwood was killed, and the hosts note he had reportedly scared a couple in a carriage.

segments.title: Smith's sentence and royal pardon
segments.summary: Smith was initially sentenced to hang, but King George III granted him a full pardon.

segments.title: Other ghost types: armor, chains, skeletons
segments.summary: Josh contrasts the bedsheet ghost with other ghost traditions such as armored ghosts like Hamlet's father, Jacob Marley in chains, and skeleton ghosts, saying the sheet-draped figure became the universal image.

segments.title: Nineteenth-century sheets as burial wrap and spiritualism
segments.summary: In the 1800s, the poor were wrapped in their bedsheets for burial, cementing the image. Late nineteenth-century spiritualists used double-exposed photos with sheet-wearing figures to fake ghosts.

segments.title: Mediums, rigs, and stage ghosts
segments.summary: Mediums used rigs to fake ghosts and some were prosecuted. The sheet ghost moved to the stage, where a theater scholar's polling reportedly found audiences were scarier with sheet ghosts than with white-makeup figures rattling chains.

segments.title: Cartoons and Casper
segments.summary: Children's cartoons made sheet ghosts less scary. Josh cites Mickey Mouse's 1937 Lonesome Ghosts, noting the ghosts are featureless and look like they are made of sheet, and the hosts jokingly suggest Casper is a kid in a sheet.

segments.title: Halloween costume tips and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about sheet costumes, with frayed sheets suggested as scarier and Chuck planning a lazy unironed one. They sign off wishing a happy Halloween.
